title: Wire the NestJS module graph
description: Place each NestJS building block onto the correct slot in the archive-api module graph from lesson 9.

widgetConfig.prompt: Drop each piece onto its correct role in the MikroORM + NestJS wiring. The lesson uses MikroOrmModule.forRoot once at the AppModule, forFeature per feature module, and @CreateRequestContext for non-HTTP entry points.

slots.label: AppModule — registers the global ORM connection + middleware
BookModule — exposes the Book repository to its services
BookController -> BookService — auto-forked EM per HTTP request
ArticleRebuildCron.run() — non-HTTP entry, needs its own EM fork

nodes.label: MikroOrmModule.forRoot(config)
nodes.hint: Once at the AppModule. Owns the connection pool and the RequestContext middleware.

nodes.label: MikroOrmModule.forFeature([Book])
nodes.hint: Per feature module — makes the @InjectRepository tokens available.

nodes.label: RequestContext middleware (auto-installed by forRoot)
nodes.hint: Forks the EM per HTTP request — without this, every handler shares the global EM.

nodes.label: @CreateRequestContext()
nodes.hint: Method decorator for queue handlers, @Cron jobs, and other non-HTTP entry points.

nodes.label: @Transactional()
nodes.hint: Method decorator that wraps the method body in em.transactional().

modelAnswer: forRoot registers the connection + the RequestContext middleware globally; forFeature exposes per-entity repositories to a feature module. RequestContext middleware forks the EM per HTTP request automatically. For anything that isn't an HTTP request — cron, queue handlers, CLI commands — you must add @CreateRequestContext() manually, otherwise the global EM is shared across runs. @Transactional() goes on the service method that owns the transaction boundary, never on the controller.

title: Fill the Transactional Outbox skeleton
description: From lesson 9's Transactional Outbox example: BookService writes a Book and an OutboxEvent in the same transaction. Fill the three blanks that the lesson highlights as load-bearing.

blanks.placeholder: send pending changes in one transaction

modelAnswer: @Transactional() wraps the service method in em.transactional() — Book + OutboxEvent land or roll back together. @CreateRequestContext() on the cron drain() forks a fresh EM for each run, so stale entities from a previous run never bleed in. em.flush() at the end of drain() commits all the `processedAt` updates in one transaction.

title: Transactional Outbox — design, implement, stress-test (AI-resilient)
description:
Design and implement a minimal Transactional Outbox for the archive-api NestJS app, and ship it as a PR. When a Book is created, an OutboxEvent entity (eventType, payload JSON, processedAt nullable) must be inserted in the same transaction as the Book INSERT. A background processor (a NestJS @Cron job decorated with @CreateRequestContext()) must poll for unprocessed events, process them (for this task: console.log the payload), and mark them processedAt. Run two book creations and verify via psql that two OutboxEvent rows exist with processedAt filled.

In the PR description, include: (1) the design — the entity relationship as a text table, the invariant this pattern guarantees, and what problem it solves that 'publish event after flush' does not; (2) the verification query output; (3) a stress-test analysis — what happens if the @Cron job crashes between reading and marking processedAt (processed twice or dropped?), and how you would make processing idempotent.

Submit the link to your branch or PR.
modelAnswer: Invariant: 'a Book exists in the DB iff its book.created event is durably recorded in OutboxEvent' — guaranteed because both INSERTs share one transaction. 'Publish after flush' breaks if the process crashes between flush and publish: the row exists, the event is lost. Crash between read-and-mark in the drain: the event is processed twice (at-least-once delivery). Idempotency requires a stable event id consumed downstream with a dedup table, or upsert-by-id at the consumer. The boundary nobody mentions: the ORM transaction does not extend to the message broker — outbox is the seam where you accept 'at-least-once' as the price of crash-safety.
